title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Dowagiac neighbors sue over nonstop crypto data center whine amid statewide pushback.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Today we're digging into the growing noise complaints from data centers, starting with a lawsuit filed by residents in Dowagiac.
That's right, Graham. Neighbors there say the high-pitched whine from Alliance Cloud Services has made their yards and open windows unusable for two years now.
The company has already been fined under Dowagiac's new noise limits, and they're planning to seal vents after switching to AI operations.
But residents are demanding real soundproofing or even buyouts. This feels like it could set a precedent for other communities dealing with similar issues.
Exactly. Data centers have been expanding fast across Michigan, bringing jobs and tax revenue but also these quality-of-life headaches like constant noise, heavy power use, and water demands.
How did we get here? It seems like just a few years ago these facilities were mostly welcomed, but now towns are pushing back hard.
The history shows a rapid buildout driven by AI and cloud computing needs. Companies look for cheap land, cool climates, and reliable power in places like the Upper Peninsula and rural counties.
And now we're seeing the downsides hit home for residents. What does this mean for electric bills if demand keeps climbing?
State regulators told lawmakers that new policies could actually help lower electricity rates even with more data centers online, depending on how the legislature handles power planning.
That's interesting. So it's not automatic that bills go up?
Not necessarily, but it depends on smart infrastructure choices and who pays for upgrades. Residents in multiple counties are watching closely as projects get proposed.
Water use is another big one I've heard about. How much does a typical facility pull?
It varies, but large ones can strain local supplies, especially in areas worried about aquifers. That's why places like East Lansing extended their moratorium to protect water quality.
Farmland and open spaces are also at stake. These facilities take up a lot of room and can change the character of small towns.
Right. Chippewa County just approved a full 12-month moratorium to study power, water, and zoning impacts before anything moves forward.
That's a rural Upper Peninsula county getting a temporary shield. How many other places are doing something similar right now?
Several. Wixom is drafting new zoning rules on noise, setbacks, and power lines before its moratorium expires. Corunna adopted an ordinance with clear limits on noise, traffic, and power.
And Ypsilanti Township rejected a University of Michigan proposal over zoning and resident concerns about power and water.
Garfield Township in Grand Traverse County is weighing its own year-long freeze, with planners set to show why old rules can't handle today's large facilities.
It sounds like a wave of local action. What happens next if these lawsuits and moratoriums keep spreading?
More townships could follow suit, forcing companies to negotiate better mitigation or look elsewhere. A win for residents in Dowagiac might encourage similar suits.
Or companies might invest in better soundproofing and site selection from the start.
That's the hope. The Dowagiac case tests whether existing noise rules can actually rein in hyperscale operations.
And if it sets a precedent, it could ripple across the state.
Meanwhile, regulators are signaling that lawmakers have tools to manage costs amid the growth.
So the big picture is communities gaining leverage through zoning and legal action while the state looks at broader policy.
We'll keep tracking how these play out.
Now for some quick hits on other developments today.
Michigan regulators told lawmakers new policies could lower power prices even as data centers grow demand.
Residents might see bill impacts depending on legislative action on planning.
Chippewa County approved a 12-month moratorium on new data center proposals to study impacts.
That pause gives officials time before any large projects advance in the rural county.
Wixom city council is drafting zoning rules on noise and setbacks just before its moratorium deadline.
Residents there have pushed for stronger protections near homes.
Corunna adopted a new ordinance with limits on noise, traffic, and power use for future centers.
It gives nearby communities a template if proposals pop up.
Ypsilanti Township rejected a University of Michigan data center site over zoning and resident concerns.
The university may look for another location or scale back.
Garfield Township planners are forwarding findings for an 18-month pause to avoid issues like those in other townships.
Northern Michigan communities are seeing rising developer interest.
Yesterday East Lansing extended its moratorium to March to block potential aquifer pollution.
That gives time for new zoning to protect neighborhoods.
Now let's look at what's on deck for listeners who want to get involved.
Tonight Negaunee City Council or Planning Commission has a public hearing on a proposed data center ordinance.
It would limit facilities to mining and industrial zones with noise and height standards.
Also today the Michigan for Responsible Data Centers Coalition is holding a virtual town hall on Van Buren Township construction and regulations.
On Monday the Kalamazoo City Commission will vote on a resolution for a temporary moratorium.
Those are real opportunities for residents to weigh in.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Dowagiac Residents Sue Over Data Center Noise as Michigan Towns Tighten Rules
